definitions.definition: The one reality, consciousness that is both light and reflexive awareness, free, performing the five acts, transcending and containing the thirty-six tattvas.

equivalents.note: Both name a non-dual conscious absolute; the Kashmir Śaivas insist theirs is active (vimarśa, svātantrya) and object to an inactive Brahman and to the world as vivarta

definitions.definition: The Unsurpassed: the supreme reality of the Trika, identified with the letter A and with the Heart; Parātrīśikā's question concerns how the anuttara grants immediate Kaula perfection.

literal: unsurpassed; that beyond which there is nothing

definitions.definition: The supreme Śiva as the Trika names him; his true form is indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess, not the forms with parts described for meditation (VBT 7-16).
In the Śiva Sūtra the upsurge of awareness (udyama) is Bhairava (1.5).

literal: the Terrible; (etym. in VBT 130) he who makes all resound through fear, gives all, pervades all

definitions.definition: Consciousness as free power, the cause of the universe (PH 1); contracted, it is the individual and the mind (PH 4-5); its essence is reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13).
Consciousness as the self (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); Kṣemarāja: the absolute freedom of knowing and doing.
Consciousness as the one reality and as each act of awareness; in the Krama the goddess is one's own consciousness (svasaṃvid).
The Lord to be recognized as one's own self: the knower and agent, established from the beginning, full of the undivided awareness 'I am this' (ĪPK 1.1.2, 4.1).
The supreme Self, whose sovereignty is the reflexive awareness that is supreme speech (ĪPK 1.5.13).
The light of consciousness by which anything appears; never without vimarśa, else it would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).
The self-reflective awareness that is the very nature of manifestation (ĪPK 1.5.11), supreme speech and the Lord's primary freedom (1.5.13); pure knowing and acting are the Lord's vimarśa (1.8.11).

The dynamic, vibrant nature of the ultimate - Śaṅkara's opening and closing of the eyes (SK 1.1); the universal vibration on which all particular vibrations rest (SK 1.19); discoverable in intense states (1.22).
Utpaladeva calls consciousness 'sphurattā', the great being, the Heart of the Supreme (ĪPK 1.5.14).

equivalents.standpoint: Kṣemarāja's synthesis of Spanda and Pratyabhijñā
equivalents.note: spanda as the dynamic side of consciousness = vimarśa / svātantrya

definitions.definition: The universal vibration on which the particular vibrations (of the guṇas etc.) rest (SK 1.19).
One's own nature, the spanda principle, from which the perceiver never departs (SK 1.3, 1.11).
Name of Śiva in the Spandakārikā's opening: by his unmeṣa and nimeṣa the world dissolves and arises (1.1).
The opening-out of spanda: that from which a new thought arises in one absorbed in one thought (SK 3.9); with nimeṣa, the pulse of creation and dissolution (1.1).
Īśvara is the outward unmeṣa, Sadāśiva the inward nimeṣa (ĪPK 3.1.3).
The closing phase of Śaṅkara's pulse (SK 1.1).
Two modes of absorption: inward, eyes-closed absorption and outward absorption in which the world is seen as consciousness; 'again and again there is merging' (Śiva Sūtra 3.45, Kṣemarāja).

notes: Pairing of the two samādhis follows Kṣemarāja's commentaries (low confidence on details).

definitions.definition: The absolute freedom of consciousness - its primary sovereignty, identical with reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13); by it the world is manifested (PH 1-2).

equivalents.note: ĪPK 1.5.13 identifies reflexive awareness as the primary freedom

definitions.definition: An appearance manifested by consciousness within itself as if external (ĪPK 1.5.1); the world is ābhāsa, real as manifestation; the individual too manifests (ābhāsana) as the first of his five acts (PH 11).

notes: Contrasted by the tradition with Advaita's vivarta (see dsp:causation, dsp:world-real-or-appearance).

definitions.definition: The universe as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness, appearing distinct yet undivided from it (TĀ 3; Paramārthasāra 12-13).
The Heart of the Supreme: consciousness as vibrancy and great being (ĪPK 1.5.14).
The Heart of Bhairava, the seed in which the universe lies like a tree in a banyan seed (Parātrīśikā 24); also the heart-centre of meditation (VBT 49).
The Heart-mantra of Bhairava taught in the Parātrīśikā (identified by the commentators as SAUḤ), in which the universe lies in seed form.
The central consciousness whose unfolding yields the bliss of consciousness (PH 17).
The middle between two breaths, cognitions or states, where reality shines (VBT 26, 61-62, 103).

equivalents.note: the central channel is one sense of madhya (VBT 35; Śiva Sūtra 3.44)

definitions.definition: Power, never different from its possessor; the door (mukha) through which Śiva is known (VBT 18-21).
The circle of the powers of consciousness; union with it withdraws the universe (Śiva Sūtra 1.6); Śaṅkara is its source (SK 1.1); the established yogin is its lord (SK 3.19).
The power of will, first of the three powers; in the Trika the goddess Parā; the Śiva Sūtra calls it Umā, the virgin (1.13).
Knowledge: as the Lord's power, one of the three; as limited knowing, bondage (Śiva Sūtra 1.2); as right knowledge, the sole cause of liberation (TĀ 1.22).
The Lord's power of action, his creatorhood, making things appear by his will (ĪPK 2.4.1).
Bliss as the power of the Lord and as the relish of consciousness in pleasure, reunion, taste and song (VBT 65-74); seven grades in the contemplation of the breath (TĀ 5.43-52).
The bliss of consciousness gained by unfolding the centre, which, made firm, is liberation in life (PH 16-17).
The perfect I-awareness whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20).
The supreme 'I', spanning the letters from A (Śiva) to HA (Śakti) joined by the bindu (PTV).
Consciousness as reflexive awareness is supreme speech, arising of itself (ĪPK 1.5.13); higher than paśyantī.
The grammarians' highest level of speech; for Somānanda it is only the knowledge-power at the Sadāśiva level, not the ultimate (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1).
The unstruck sound in which one is immersed to reach the supreme Brahman (VBT 38).
The grammarians' absolute, refuted as final by Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 2).
The highest of the Trika's three goddesses; Bhairava's own state proclaimed as the Goddess (VBT 17); the power of will (TĀ 1.271-272).
The supreme Kālī of the Krama, the last of the goddesses of cognition.
In Abhinavagupta's Trika the fourth goddess above Parā, Parāparā and Aparā.
The goddess as the power of kalana - projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding - in twelve phases of cognition (TĀ 4.148-173).

literal: the Dark One; she who is time / reckons

definitions.definition: The activity of consciousness named by the root kal: projecting (kṣepa), knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).
The nameless phase beyond emission, persistence and withdrawal in the Krama sequence.
One's own awareness, unbounded and complete, to be realized (the Mata line quoted at TĀ 4.263a).
One of the thirty-six levels of manifestation from Śiva to earth (Paramārthasāra 11; PH 7).
First tattva: pure consciousness (cit), the 'I'.
Second tattva: the power of Śiva, bliss (ānanda).
Third tattva: will predominant; the inward 'nimeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'I am this' with the 'I' prominent.
Fourth tattva: knowledge predominant; the outward 'unmeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'this am I' with the 'this' prominent.
Fifth tattva: action predominant; the co-reference of 'I' and 'this' in balance (ĪPK 3.1.3); its rise gives mastery of the wheel of powers (Śiva Sūtra 1.21).

Sixth tattva: the Lord's power of concealment - 'the supreme freedom of Maheśa which accomplishes the impossible' (Paramārthasāra 15) - making the knowable appear as separate; real as a power, not an inexplicable illusion.
Kañcuka: limited agency ('only a little I do').
Kañcuka: limited knowledge ('only this I know').
Kañcuka: attachment, the sense of lacking something.
Kañcuka: time, limiting to sequence ('only now').
Kañcuka: restriction of cause and place ('only this, here').
Twelfth tattva: consciousness bound by māyā and the five kañcukas; the limited individual subject.
The five (with māyā, six) sheaths that limit the individual: kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati (Paramārthasāra 16-17).
Impurity, which is ignorance - the cause of the sprouting of saṃsāra (MVT 1.23; TĀ 1.23); not a substance.
The impurity of individuality: loss of freedom by awareness, or awareness without freedom (ĪPK 3.2.4); 'limited knowledge is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.2).

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: The impurity of difference: the appearance of the knowable as separate (ĪPK 3.2.5).

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: The impurity of action in an unconscious agent (ĪPK 3.2.5).

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: Not the absence of knowledge but incomplete manifestation of the knowable (TĀ 1.25-26); twofold, in the intellect and in the person, the latter the root of saṃsāra (Tantrasāra 1).
The contraction of consciousness into the individual (PH 4, 9).
Conceptual cognition by exclusion of an opposite (ĪPK 1.6.5); dream is vikalpa (Śiva Sūtra 1.9); its dissolution is a means (PH 18) and its purification the śākta way (TĀ 4).
The thought-free condition repeatedly invoked in the dhāraṇās (VBT 26, 43, 45, 108).
One of the Lord's three powers with cognition and memory (ĪPK 1.3.7); every determinate awareness arises by exclusion of an opposite (1.6.5) - a reworking of the Buddhist apoha.
The bound soul, deprived of his glory by the kalās and made the object of the powers of the mass of sounds (SK 3.13).
The totality of the letters, whose powers bind the unaware and grant perfection to the aware (SK 3.13-16).
The subtle body arising from the subtle elements and consisting of mind, ego and intellect, which confines the individual (SK 3.17).
Agitation whose subsidence reveals the supreme state (SK 1.9).
Agency, imperishable, as opposed to effect-hood, which perishes (SK 1.14).
Consciousness descended and contracted by the knowable (PH 5); turned inward, it becomes consciousness again (PH 13).
The bound self is the mind (Śiva Sūtra 3.1); the mind is mantra (2.1).
Mind and the rest, which one contemplates as absent in oneself (VBT 94).
The notion 'I' and 'mine', at whose arising the mind is to go to the supportless (VBT 131); in the Krama it is dissolved in the phases of Kālāgnirudra and Mahākāla (TĀ 4.161-168).
The doors of pleasure and pain, to be abandoned for abiding in the self (VBT 136); in the Śiva Sūtra, the spectators of the self's dance (3.11).
Latent impressions, exhausted when the mind subsides in the supportless (VBT 82, 'kṣīṇāśaya').
The correlated objects and subjects that make the universe manifold (PH 3).
The yogin's distinction is attentiveness to their relation (VBT 106).
Waking is [external] cognition (Śiva Sūtra 1.8).
Dream is thought-constructs (Śiva Sūtra 1.9).
Deep sleep is non-discrimination, māyā (Śiva Sūtra 1.10); a void absorption like deep sleep is not the goal (SK 1.12-13).
The fourth state, whose enjoyment arises amid the three (Śiva Sūtra 1.7) and which is to be poured like oil into them (3.20).
The fourth abode in which emission, maintenance, withdrawal and the three states shine without covering it (Paramārthasāra 34-35).

equivalents.note: the Māṇḍūkya's fourth; the Kashmir Śaivas add turyātīta and require the fourth to pervade the three

definitions.definition: The state beyond the fourth, in which the fourth pervades all states completely (Tantrāloka 10; Kṣemarāja).
The knower with all three impurities, identifying with body and objects (waking).
The knower resting in the void, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution, with the kārma impurity (ĪPK 3.2.8).
The knower of pure awareness without agency (ĪPK 3.2.6-7).
The knower at the level of śuddhavidyā.
The knower at the level of Īśvara.
The knower at the level of Sadāśiva.
Firm realization of oneness with consciousness even while body and the rest are experienced (PH 16).
One who sees the whole world as play is liberated in life (SK 2.5).
Though living he is liberated, though acting not stained (VBT 142); liberated though joined to a body (Paramārthasāra 61).
Not an abode or a going elsewhere, but the manifestation of one's own power by cutting the knot of ignorance (Paramārthasāra 60); one, whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-166).
Recognition of one's own self as the Lord, shown by revealing his powers (ĪPK 1.1.3); like recognizing a lover standing near (4.17).
Immersion in Rudra's power, of three kinds - āṇava, śākta, śāmbhava (MVT 2.21-23).
The means to immersion: anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava; liberation is one whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-170).
The 'means-less': realization by the teacher's word alone for the most intensely graced (TĀ 2).
The divine means: immersion without thought through the teacher's awakening (MVT 2.23).
The empowered means: contemplation with the mind alone, purifying thought (MVT 2.22; TĀ 4).
The individual means: breath, bodily seals, visualization, letters and places (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).
The descent of the Lord's power, independent of karma, intense, middling or mild in three degrees each (TĀ 13); its signs in MVT 2.14-16.

Initiation, in many forms (TĀ 14-22); for one who knows the Heart, initiation needs no sesame and ghee (Parātrīśikā 25); Spanda calls identification with the meditated 'the initiation of nirvāṇa' (SK 2.7).
'The teacher is the means' (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); from the teacher comes awakening to the wheel of letters (2.7).
The observances binding an initiate (TĀ 15); the Mata scriptures reject them (TĀ 4.262).

literal: conventional rule; vow of the initiate

definitions.definition: Lineage (gotra, maṭhikā); lineage-based restrictions are not enjoined in the Trika and forbidden in the Mata scriptures (TĀ 4.265-270).
One born from a Kaula union, by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra (TĀ 29.162-163).
In the Trika's Kaula dimension, the totality of the powers (Śakti) as opposed to akula (Śiva); the Kaula rule dwelling in Bhairava's heart (Parātrīśikā 4).
Śiva as beyond the kula; the Akula abode into which full consciousness finally dissolves (TĀ 4.170).
Name of the Trika scripture/tradition, placed at the top of the hierarchy of grace (TĀ 13.301).
The wondering relish of consciousness in itself; in the Śiva Sūtra 'wonder' marks the stages of yoga (1.12).
Kṣemarāja glosses the 'upsurge' that is Bhairava (Śiva Sūtra 1.5) as the flash of the supreme I-awareness.
'The upsurge is Bhairava' (Śiva Sūtra 1.5).
Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace; the individual performs them too, as manifesting, relishing, reflecting, planting the seed and dissolving (PH 10-11).
Powers arising in yoga (Śiva Sūtra 1.19-20; SK 3.1-7), which, gained under delusion, fall short of liberation (Śiva Sūtra 3.6).
Absorption that, cultivated in emergence, becomes ever-present (nityodita, PH 19); the bliss of the world is its joy (Śiva Sūtra 1.18).
The ground of limited knowledge (Śiva Sūtra 1.4); the groups of letters are presided over by Māheśvarī and the other mothers of the bound (3.19).
The letters from A to KṢA in their natural order as the emanation of the tattvas (Parātrīśikā 5-9).

literal: the 'little mother': the power of the letters

definitions.definition: The alphabet in a scrambled order (beginning NA and ending PHA), with vowels and consonants mixed, uniting Śiva and Śakti; the name of the Mālinīvijayottara's goddess.
Letter or sound as object of contemplation (VBT 30, 40, 81, 90) and as an āṇava support (MVT 2.21).
The emissive power of the Goddess (VBT 24) and the letter ḥ at whose end awareness is placed (VBT 91).
The point of light seen or meditated (VBT 36-37) and a subtle phase of a mantra's utterance (VBT 42, 90).
The subtle resonance of a mantra and the self-arising sound which is itself the mantra repeated (VBT 42, 145).
The unstruck, unbroken inner sound, the Sound-Brahman (VBT 38).

notes: In haṭha sources anāhata is also the heart-cakra; here the unstruck sound.

definitions.definition: The vowelless (and consonantless, ahala) sound meditated while closing ears and lower door (VBT 114); used in cutting the flows of breath (Kṣemarāja on PH 18).
Uttered and prolonged, with the void contemplated at its end (VBT 39).
The mind is mantra (Śiva Sūtra 2.1); mantras rest on the strength of spanda and dissolve in it with the worshipper's mind (SK 2.1-2).
Experienced by attending to the great lake (Śiva Sūtra 1.22); in PH 20 the perfect I-ness is the potency of the great mantra.
Repeated contemplation of the supreme state; the self-arising sound is what is repeated (VBT 144-145); the liberated's conversation is japa (Śiva Sūtra 3.27).
The mantra the living being repeats with each breath, going out with sa and in with ha (VBT 155b).
The spontaneous japa of the breath, 21,600 per day and night, the Goddess's japa (VBT 156).
Seals such as Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā and Khecarī (VBT 77; TĀ 32); an āṇava support (karaṇa).
The state of Śiva when innate knowledge arises (Śiva Sūtra 2.5).
A seal named among five (VBT 77) and a power-group in the pañcavāha.

literal: she who moves in the void (space of consciousness)
notes: Not the haṭha tongue-practice of the same name.

definitions.definition: Each of the 112 'teachings of the waveless state' of the Vijñāna Bhairava (v. 139); in the Mālinīvijayottara, concentrations on elements, subtle elements and senses (chs. 12-17).
The waveless state to which the 112 teachings lead (VBT 129, 139).
The fullness of Bhairava's state (bharitākārā, VBT 15) and of the practitioner (VBT 24, 72, 117).
Void as an object of contemplation leading beyond itself (VBT 32, 39-40, 43-48, 58): 'by the void power one goes to voidness'.
The void as a limited subject-position (śūnya-pramātṛ), subordinate to consciousness (ĪPK 3.2.12-15).
The supportless mind, body or awareness through which Bhairava is reached (VBT 80, 82, 91, 108).
The fire of the end of time, visualized rising and burning body and world (VBT 52-53).
The six paths - letters, mantras, words; kalās, tattvas, worlds - contemplated from gross to supreme (VBT 56-57; TĀ 6-12).
The breath-power (marudrūpā śakti) whose arising, turning and suspension are contemplated (VBT 24-27, 64); in the āṇava means its five forms carry the seven blisses (TĀ 5).
Prāṇa and apāna prevail in waking and dream, samāna in deep sleep, udāna in the fourth, vyāna beyond (ĪPK 3.2.19-20).
The point twelve finger-breadths beyond (above or outside) the body where the breath ends and the mind is to be cast (VBT 28, 50-51).
The central channel meditated as fine as a lotus fibre (VBT 35).
The path in which the in- and out-breaths set (SK 1.24); Śiva Sūtra 3.44 makes the inner centre prior to the three channels.
Channels whose withdrawal is a yogic attainment (Śiva Sūtra 3.5).
The power rising from the root through the wheels to the dvādaśānta (VBT 28-29), 'curved in form' as the breath (VBT 154); the Trika distinguishes its forms as power of breath and of consciousness.

notes: The word kuṇḍalinī itself is not in VBT 28-29 (the text says 'śakti'); the identification is the commentators'.

definitions.definition: Centres through which the power rises (VBT 29); the Netratantra names six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Netra 7.1).
Retention, at whose end, as at the end of exhalation or inhalation, the Peaceful shines (VBT 27).
The first āṇava support: the breath contemplated in its movement (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).

Devotion as the relish of identity with Śiva; for the one rich in devotion Śiva manifests without meditation or procedure (Śivastotrāvalī 1.1); the intense devotion of the dispassionate is Śaṅkara's power (VBT 121).
Not with flowers but the firm mind fixed on the great void (VBT 147); the liberated worships Bhairava with the substances of self-awareness (Paramārthasāra 75).
The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the bound self is the mind (3.1); the self is a dancer (3.9).
